source_refs.note: Topic printed as 2.4.1, printed page 26: emission and absorption spectra (Figures 2.2 and 2.3).

blocks.text: When an element in its gaseous state is heated to a high temperature or subjected to an electrical discharge, radiation of certain wavelengths is emitted. The spectrum of this radiation contains coloured lines and is the atomic emission spectrum. When a beam of white light passes through a gaseous sample of the element in the cold state, certain wavelengths are absorbed, and the absorbed wavelengths show up as dark lines: the atomic absorption spectrum. The wavelengths of the dark lines in the absorption spectrum are exactly the same as those of the coloured lines in the emission spectrum.

Each element has a unique arrangement of electrons and so a unique set of fixed energy levels. The wavelengths and frequencies of the radiation absorbed or emitted when electrons jump from one energy level to another must therefore be unique too, so every element has its own characteristic spectrum and is identified by it: atomic spectra are the fingerprints of the elements.

blocks.alt: Two horizontal bands. The upper, black, carries four bright lines, red at 656 nm, blue-green at 486 nm, blue at 434 nm and violet at 410 nm, the emission spectrum of hydrogen. The lower is a rainbow from violet to red with black lines at the same four positions, the absorption spectrum.
blocks.caption: The emission and absorption spectra of hydrogen (original diagram after Figures 2.2 and 2.3).
blocks.long_description: A hot or electrically excited gas emits only certain wavelengths, which appear as coloured lines on a dark background; for hydrogen the visible lines are at 656, 486, 434 and 410 nm. When white light passes through the cold gas the same wavelengths are absorbed and appear as dark lines in the continuous spectrum. Because every element has its own fixed energy levels, its lines are unique, and the spectrum identifies the element.

blocks.prompt: Why do the dark lines of the absorption spectrum fall at exactly the wavelengths of the bright lines of the emission spectrum?
blocks.explanation: Both come from the same fixed energy levels of the atom. In emission an electron drops from a higher level to a lower one and gives out a photon of exactly that energy difference; in absorption an electron takes in a photon of the same energy to make the reverse jump. Same levels, same differences, same wavelengths.

items: Emission spectrum: coloured lines from a hot or electrically excited gas. Absorption spectrum: dark lines where a cold gas absorbs white light; same wavelengths (hydrogen: 656, 486, 434, 410 nm).
Each element's fixed energy levels give it a unique spectrum, its fingerprint.
